newsitem.title: USA: Analysts see Mich. pension plan as credit neutral.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Mich. pension plan as credit neutral.

text.p: Some rating analyts said Friday that Michigan's possible plan to issue around $3.5 billion of taxable pension bonds to fully fund the school employees retirement system would be a neutral for the state's credit.
"It can be more of a neutral unfunded liability," said Joe O'Keefe, a director at Standard & Poor's Corp. "You're replacing a more nebulous obligation with one that sticks."
O'Keefe said that by selling bonds, the state may face some investment risk in managing the money.
"So we have to see what they come up with. My feeling is there may be some marginal risk, but no significant change in the financial posture of the state," he added.
Claire Cohen, vice chair of Fitch Investors Service Inc, said the plan would be neither a positive nor a negative for the state.
She added that when Michigan Treasurer Doug Roberts described the plan to her, she did not hear anything "to give me concern."

Roberts said Friday the state was exploring the pension bond issue on both legislative and legal fronts to see if it could be accomplished. He also said that the bonds would have to be sold at an interest rate of less than eight percent to make the plan work from an actuarial standpoint.
Robert Kurtter, an analyst at Moody's Investors Service Inc, said the agency would have to see the details of the plan and whether the pension debt would constitute state debt.
Roberts said the bonds may be backed by annual state appropriations and school districts' annual pension contribution of 3.6 percent of their annual payroll may be used to pay debt service.

However, the treasurer also said that officials were examining legal matters to determine if the pension debt would be considered state debt. As state debt, the bonds would need voter approval, he said.

Kurtter said Moody's general view of pension obligation bonds was that they substitute a fixed obligation for a somewhat flexible obligation, where the size and timing of payments can be moved or changed.
The pension bond plan is likely to win support from Michigan school districts, according to Ray Telman, associate executive director of the Michigan Association of School Administrators.
"I think without exception, the school community will embrace (the plan)," he said.
Telman said the plan would stabilize the district's pension obligations and pay off the unfunded liability at a lower interest rate.
School districts assumed responsibility for the retirement system in the wake of a 1993 overhaul of school funding in Michigan.
